newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan tries tough tack to limit diplomatic losses.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan tries tough tack to limit diplomatic losses.

text.p: Taiwan scrambled on Monday to limit damage from the surprise loss of a stalwart diplomatic friend, telling its handful of cash-strapped allies they would feel pain if they switched recognition to rival China.
In a surprise announcement late on Sunday, Taipei said it was ending links with the Bahamas after learning the Caribbean nation was preparing to exchange ties with Beijing.
Rather than waiting helplessly for Nassau to act, Taipei moved decisively, announcing that all treaties with the Bahamas were suspended and recalling its ambassador.
Foreign Minister John Chang said the brusque treatment was intended as a signal to other allies that they had much to lose if they followed suit and recognised communist China.

"One of the reasons we did this was to prevent a domino effect from happening," Chang told a news briefing. "We hope neighbouring (Latin American) nations understand that the Republic of China is a sovereign nation with dignity."

After the Bahamian shift, Taiwan will have ties with only 30 states, most of them small, poor and heavily dependent on Taipei's financial largesse. The number soon will fall to 29, as top ally South Africa has said it would switch ties in 1997.
Since a civil war split them in 1949, Beijing has regarded Taiwan as a renegade province ineligible for diplomatic ties and has pressed to bring the Nationalist bastion under its control.

Analysts said Taipei's blunt response toward the Bahamas may reflect a shift away from its much-criticised "silver-dollar" diplomacy -- doling out cash to ensure foreign relations -- at a time when Beijing is squeezing Taiwan's allies politically.
Taiwan's pre-emptive severing of ties contrasted sharply to its response to Pretoria's shock November announcement that it was abandoning Taipei in favour of Beijing.

Taipei begged and pleaded with Pretoria, reportedly offering to sweeten the terms of their longtime alliance. South Africa was happy to maintain economic relations but refused to reverse its decision on diplomatic ties.

"The government (now) may not want to pay too much a price if it is certain that a diplomatic ally is preparing to set up official relations with the mainland," said National Taiwan University political analyst Lu Ya-li.
Another National Taiwan University expert, Chang Lin-cheng, said Taiwan, despite its vast wealth, was discovering that it was no longer a match for an economically resurgent China.
"Besides offering more aid to our cash-strapped allies, the Chinese communists are more influential in the world than we are," Chang said.
"It's worth pondering whether we should continue to spend a huge amount of money in securing ties with some allies which intend to switch ties to Beijing," she added.

Professor Chang said Beijing was placing intense political and economic pressure on countries recognising Taiwan, notifying them that their Hong Kong consulates must close after the British colony reverts to Chinese rule on July 1.
The Bahamas, Panama, Costa Rica and several other Taiwan allies have such consulates as well as strong trade interests in Hong Kong that they are loathe to abandon.
China's diplomatic squeeze may be bearing fruit.
The Bahamas and two other staunch Taiwanese allies, Panama and Costa Rica, failed to support Taiwan's ill-fated bid to enter the World Health Organisation, a U.N. body.

Taipei's respected United Daily News quoted a source as saying Panama asked Taiwan to "take full responsibility" after Beijing cut off trade and investment there, and said Taipei must offer guaranties for similar losses in Hong Kong.
The newspaper quoted sources as saying Taiwan planned to appropriate T$4 billion (US$140 million) to help secure ties with Panama and six other Latin American allies.
Panama's Taipei ambassador, Carlos Mendoza, said on Monday that Taiwanese investments in Panama were expected to exceed US$100 million before the end of 1997.
